title: Appropriateness is all you need! General-purpose chatbots and what they may and may not say
benchmark_measurement: The paper does not introduce a new benchmark for religion. It uses a specific example—a model's refusal to answer a tautological question about the religion of a hypothetical 'first Jewish President'—to illustrate how current safety mechanisms can lead to overly cautious and logically flawed responses when dealing with protected attributes like religion.
findings: The paper finds that models like ChatGPT are hard-wired to avoid commenting on personal features, including religion, to such an extent that they fail to process simple, tautological questions involving religious identity. This behavior, termed 'milquetoasting', is presented as a key limitation of the prevailing 'safety-normativity' approach in chatbot design.
